- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The 44-year-old arrived on Merseyside with a glowing coaching reputation after three seasons at Bournemouth, the last of which saw the south coast club secure their highest-ever Premier League finish of sixth place.
In a new series called 'Boss with Jamie Carragher', Iraola tells the former Liverpool captain how he aims to turn around the club's fortunes after they lost 12 times in the top flight last season to finish fifth in the table, 12 months on from being crowned champions, as well as explaining in depth his coaching philosophy and how long it may take his players to adapt.
And the new man also looks ahead to his first competitive match as Liverpool boss when he takes his team to what is sure to be a bouncing St James' Park on Sunday afternoon in a game you can see live on Sky Sports Premier League.
At the moment, Liverpool supporters are getting a little bit nervous because of the lack of activity in the transfer market, so can you assure them you will you sign some players before the end of this transfer window?
We'll definitely sign players, yes. I hope more than one. The thing is, me as a coach selfishly, I want the players for the first day of pre-season so everyone is ready to go, but also I understand how this works.
Some days you have to wait until the end. The important picture is the one we have on September 1 and I hope, because it's true that we are still quite thin, that we can have more help from here until the end of the market.
What's the difference in getting players over the line for Liverpool compared to Bournemouth?
Probably the money, the level of the player is different, but the issues normally are the same.
Some deals you cannot do in the beginning, you have to wait and you have your hopes of 'let's think that this is possible. It's not possible today, maybe it's going to be possible later' and you have to be patient as a manager.
You learn with experience. Probably the first summers are very hard because you want your team ready to go straight away, but at the end, for me, the key is once the market is finished, we are happy with the team that we have.
Something that really fascinated me a couple of years ago about your team was a quote from Pep Guardiola, talking about your team and other teams in the Premier League, saying this is the future of football - do you agree?
I think you have to read the moments [in games]. For me, the key is to believe in the things that you are doing.
I think I'm here because the way we want to play is quite clear and you can identify it. And as you said, I'm not new in the league. More or less, the players, when you arrive, they suspect what you are going to demand from them.
This cannot change too much. I will need to adapt to be in Liverpool and to sometimes control a little bit more the games, if you want, but now I prefer to make mistakes, probably going more towards the other side than to more control situations, because I know that it's easier to fix than opposite.
You're going to have to learn to have maybe more control, so do you have to alter your training around that and do things slightly differently because you are managing one of the big boys rather than someone coming up against the bigger teams?
Yes that's mandatory because the same exercise with the Liverpool players, it evolves differently without me giving any different instruction because they play in a different way because there is more control naturally in the exercises.
The teams have certain tempos with the ball, certain tempos without the ball, and this is very difficult to change. I have to be the one not changing a little bit. We are used to doing these things.
Let's take the positive things about this, but we need something also different and that's what we are trying to do.
What I find interesting about your team, because you're very famous for pressing and how your teams are off the ball and you have a mixture, like a hybrid sort of system, of at times man-to-man marking and at other times, zone marking?
It's true, I always say, if you go straight away man to man, most of the teams will play long and then it's a matter of winning the second balls.
I want if they go long, to have one more than them so I want sometimes to give the plus one, but also you have to be aggressive enough to sometimes arrive to man-to-man situations. There is a lot of interpretation there in between, some players have to live in between opposition players, when it's worth it to risk and jump when it's not worth it.
It's not going to be the same against all the opposition, some positions you have to invite them to play more, others they will play, so you have to be even more aggressive.
This is the cat and mouse game we always play and the more we play, the more the players understand what we are trying to do. I think it's going to get better, but we have to go through these processes.
Your system at Bournemouth was fantastic. Obviously we've seen the results each year getting better, but you had a difficult start when you first went into Bournemouth. Does that show your way of playing, or in terms of without the ball, is it a lot of training work, a lot to get into the players and is it almost going to take time for that to come to fruition with Liverpool?
It's not just me, you can feel straight away the teams that have had the same manager for three, four, five seasons, they do the basics already very well, and then they add certain things from season to season.
But there is a structure, there is a floor in that team that always the performance will be, there will be a minimum.
That's the advantage, when you are in a place in the first year, you have to change a lot of things. Second year, you already have a base of players that already know it, they will help the ones that are in the third year, and my last two projects have been three years in Rayo Vallecano, three years in Bournemouth, so normally you go [about] improving, but I know also this is Liverpool, they are not going to wait 10 games until this gets going.
I know these demands and I want to think we are going to be probably not 100 per cent on Sunday, but good enough to get results.
I've seen a quote from you in that you said you didn't enjoy your playing career with Athletic Club as much as you should, or you were too hard on yourself, because it was your club and that's exactly what I used to think when I was a player at Liverpool?
When you play for your club, you feel responsible of everything and you think everyone is looking at you in every second, every moment.
You have to be perfect. You have to show the face that in that moment and you don't really play free - you overthink everything. You lose and you spend two days thinking 'I don't want to go to the street, I don't want to see anyone', and you don't really enjoy it.
I always say that I've enjoyed more my time as a manager because of this, because I think when you leave playing, there are one, two, three years when you understand maybe it wasn't as important. If you stop playing, nobody cares.
Now a lot of people don't recognise you and you regret a little bit not really having enjoyed those moments, because they are not going to come again. We cannot play anymore. Now it's probably late, and I wouldn't like this to happen when I'm a coach.
That's probably one of the things why I'm ready almost to take risks, because I don't feel that pressure that I felt when I was playing.
You mentioned about being a manager and taking more risk - would you class yourself as one of the riskier, you go for it more on the front foot and are more proactive?
I don't want also to be riskier. Riskier sounds like you are not effective - our approach is because we think it's the best way to win. I prefer to be a good team and win things than to be entertaining.
A lot of people say 'it's very entertaining to see', but I always say, I prefer that you tell me 'you are very good, you are solid' and I want to think that our teams and my teams always have been quite organised. They talk a lot about this chaos, but there is a lot of organisation there - there is a purpose on everything.
Everyone in the team, I want them to know what they are doing, but also what the team-mates are supposed to do, so when something doesn't work, everyone looks at the same player like, 'you should be here, you should be the one' and they learn from each other and this is the point where we need to arrive.
Now that everyone understands what everyone is doing, they can sometimes even solve situations without me intervening.
When you say it will take a time to arrive to that point, can you give us a timescale - is this something that you think would take a few months to bed in?
Whenever we arrive is not the end point. We will need to keep improving and football is always like this.
The things that you are doing are not enough anymore, so you have to do something extra and you have to do something better and quicker and this is the evolution.
How fast we will arrive to certain points... I think the quicker we understand things, the more complete as a team we can be.
We can change things live in games, we don't want to wait until half-time to change things because if you are ready, everyone understands, you can just do three things, and then we change the approach.
Sometimes I love it when players come to me, and they tell me 'no, they are doing this, I think we should do this' - that's the moment where you think 'OK, now we are getting it, we are there'.
Your style of football is probably a little bit direct, or the first pass forward, so it lends itself to maybe a more transitional game - is the big challenge for you as a coach, certainly at Liverpool now, to almost have a little bit more control of the game and be less transitional?
For me, it's about having the chances for ourselves. It's not about control, it's not about the amount of possession, I want us to be the team with the chances.
I will give you an example of Monaco. We lost 2-3, we were very good in the first half. I think we had the same possession, first half and second half.
In the first half, I think we had 15 shots or something like this. We were all over them. In the second half, we had exactly the same amount of possession, 51 to 52 per cent, but they were all over us.
So, it's not a matter of if we spend more time on the ball, it's a matter of arriving and having the chances and you feel it straight away.
I think there has to be a purpose in possession, which sometimes, like a lot of teams do, we have to rest on the ball. I prefer to rest on the ball than rest without the ball, because you are the one deciding when to start playing faster, but there will be moments that we have to control every phase.
Sunday at Newcastle, big atmosphere, but a new manager who likes to be aggressive - what are your thoughts on the game?
There has been a managerial change, but they want to keep the strength of Newcastle. With xG, I think they've been very good attacking the spaces, they have one of the quickest forward lines, so they will still be very good in transition like they've been the last year.
I love the atmosphere at St James' Park, so you have to be ready for a strong start, be at the level of the game and I hope we can impose our game and control the game as long as it goes.
This is the first in a new series called 'Boss with Jamie Carragher' - In this new series, Jamie Carragher interviews some of the Premier League's top managers, beginning with Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola.
Watch Newcastle vs Liverpool live on Sky Sports Premier League and Main Event from 4pm Sunday, kick-off 4.30pm.
summary: Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola sat down with Jamie Carragher to discuss his coaching philosophy, summer transfer plans, and his upcoming Premier League season opener against Newcastle United. Iraola, who joined Liverpool after three successful seasons at Bournemouth, acknowledged that his squad is currently thin but expressed confidence that more players will be signed before the transfer window closes. He explained his tactical approach, which blends intensive pressing with a hybrid defensive structure, emphasizing that his goal is to create goalscoring chances rather than simply accumulate possession.
key_points: Andoni Iraola took over as Liverpool manager after Arne Slot following a fifth-place finish last season.
The head coach confirmed that Liverpool will sign more players before the transfer window closes.
Iraola's tactical philosophy prioritizes creating scoring chances and purposeful possession over passive control.
He employs a hybrid system combining man-to-man and zonal marking to maintain defensive aggressiveness.

title: Leandro Paredes receives 10-match ban as Argentina punished for World Cup final brawl
author: PA Media; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Three Argentina players have been banned for their part in a brawl at the end of last month’s World Cup final against Spain, but they have only been fined for displaying a Falkland Islands banner after the semi-final win over England.
Leandro Paredes has been given a 10-match ban and a $90,000 (£66,000) fine by Fifa’s disciplinary committee, while Nahuel Molina was given a seven-match suspension and fined the same amount.
Thiago Almada was given a one-match ban and a $30,000 (£22,000) fine, while from coaching staff Roberto Ayala was banned for three matches and fined the same amount. Spain’s Gavi has also been given a one-match ban and a $30,000 fine.
The Argentinian football association (AFA) has been fined $321,000 in relation to the displaying of a banner at the end of the England game. It read “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” which translates as “the Falkland Islands are Argentinian”. The fine also covered breaches by Argentina supporters of Fifa’s anti-discrimination regulations at other World Cup matches.
For the discrimination offences, the AFA has been ordered to play the country’s next home match at 50% capacity, with a 50% capacity restriction at a further match suspended. Fifa said $100,000 of the fine was also suspended.
The banner was condemned by UK politicians at the time it was displayed, with Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calling for the players who held it up to be suspended. Uefa had banned two Spain players – Rodri and Álvaro Morata – after they sang about Spain’s claims to Gibraltar after their Euro 2024 triumph.
On 6 August, the AFA announced that the date of the semi-final win over England – 15 July – would be commemorated as National Football Teams Day in the future.
summary: FIFA's disciplinary committee has banned three Argentina players following a brawl at the end of the World Cup final against Spain, with Leandro Paredes receiving the longest suspension. The Argentinian football association was also fined over a Falkland Islands banner displayed after the semi-final against England, as well as fan discrimination breaches. Additionally, Spain's Gavi received a one-match ban.
key_points: Leandro Paredes received a 10-match ban and a $90,000 fine for his part in the World Cup final brawl.
Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven matches and Thiago Almada for one match.
The Argentinian football association was fined $321,000 for displaying a Falkland Islands banner and for fan discrimination breaches.
Spain player Gavi was given a one-match ban and a $30,000 fine.
Argentina's next home match must be played at 50% capacity due to discrimination offences.

title: Arsenal 3-0 Coventry: How the players rated
author: Alex Howell
content:
![Bukayo Saka and Christos Tzolis](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/3f46/live/2b403310-9d9d-11f1-bff5-1bcd013e5a56.jpg)
Christos Tzolis put in the ball which led to Bukayo Saka scoring Arsenal's second goal
- Published
Arsenal starting XI
David Raya: The Arsenal number one was barely tested. 6
Ben White: His partnership with Bukayo Saka was back to its best and he grabbed an assist for Arsenal's third goal. 7
Cristhian Mosquera: A solid display from the centre-back, who had little to deal with. 7
Gabriel Magalhaes: Was given a tough ride by Ellis Simms at times and picked up a booking, but, on the whole, it was a comfortable evening for the Brazilian as Arsenal kept a clean sheet. 7
Riccardo Calafiori: The left-back is a key part of how Arsenal attack because of the unconventional positions he picks up. His pinpoint pass picked out Kai Havertz for the opening goal. 8
Myles Lewis-Skelly: A confident performance in the middle of pitch which makes all the talk of him potentially being sold during this transfer window look very silly. 7
Declan Rice: A trademark powerful run with the ball started the attack for Arsenal's second goal. 7
Martin Odegaard: The heartbeat of the Arsenal team. The captain had lots of bright moments as the Gunners pinned Coventry back. Scored a fortunate third but his performance deserved a goal. 8
Bukayo Saka: Looked back to his sharpest in the Community Shield last Sunday and brought that form into this game. Gave Jay Dasilva a torrid time and scored the second goal. 8
Christos Tzolis: A couple of very bright runs early on and a shot that went over the bar. It was his hard work that won the ball back for Arsenal's opening goal and his cross was palmed into Saka for the second. A constant threat all match. 9
Kai Havertz: The German international is one of Mikel Arteta's favourite players and put in his usual intelligent performance. A very good finish to give Arsenal an early lead. 8
Subs:
Martin Zubimendi (on 68, Rice): Spain's World Cup winner came on when the game was won and kept things simple in front of the Arsenal back four. 7
Noni Madueke (on 68, Saka): Not many chances to attack as Arsenal cruised to three points. 6
Eberechi Eze (on 76, Tzolis): 5
Mikel Merino (on 76, Odegaard): 5
Piero Hincapie (on 81, Calafiori): 5
Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, Gyokeres, Nwaneri, Dowman
Coventry starting XI:
Carl Rushworth: A confident take from an Arsenal corner in the first half, but will be disappointed in how he dealt with the second Arsenal goal on his Premier League debut. Rushworth was also beaten by a scuffed Odegaard shot for the third. 5
Milan Van Ewijk: Lost the ball for the Arsenal opener and his team were up against it after going behind in the 15th minute. 4
Bobby Thomas: A tough night for the Coventry centre-back, but he did react well to clear when Rushworth parried a shot in the second half. 5
Aurele Amenda: A big block to deny Bukayo Saka from the edge of the six-yard box in the first half. Tried to battle physically with Havertz but part of a back four that conceded three. 5
Jay Dasilva: Had a difficult night against Saka, who was on top of his game. One good dribble in the second half. 5
Matt Grimes: The Coventry captain tried to get on the ball when he could in midfield but was not given any time. 6
Frank Onyeka: A lot of hard work from Onyeka but unfortunately for him a lot of it was done without the ball. 5
Caleb Yirenkyi: Tried to give energy to the Coventry midfield but was overpowered by an impressive Arsenal side. Booked for a foul on Lewis-Skelly. 6
Loum Tchaouna: The winger provided some threat for Coventry on the wing and his speculative acrobatic effort in the first half had Raya panicking for a second. 6
Brandon Thomas-Asante: Coventry did not have much of the ball so the winger was not able to show much going forward. 5
Ellis Simms: The striker battled hard against Gabriel and beat him once with a nice piece of skill. 6
Subs:
Victor Torp (on 62, Yirenkyi): The game was over when the midfielder came on. 6
Taiwo Awoniyi (on 70, Simms): Given a thankless task of leading the line when his side were three goals behind. 5
Jack Rudoni (on 70, Thomas-Asante): Not any chance to make an impact. 5
Hamer (on 82, Tchaouna): 5
Subs not used: Wilson, Sakamoto, Kitching, Latibeaudiere, Eccles.
How did you rate the players?
How to play
Rate players out of 10 for this game. The rater will close 30 minutes after the final whistle. You must be signed in to a BBC account to play.
Substitutes
Substitutes
After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.
summary: Arsenal secured a comfortable 3-0 victory over Coventry, backed by strong performances across their starting lineup. Kai Havertz opened the scoring early, followed by goals from Bukayo Saka and captain Martin Odegaard. The win maintained Arsenal's control throughout the match, keeping a clean sheet against a struggling Coventry side.
key_points: Kai Havertz gave Arsenal an early lead with a very good finish from a Riccardo Calafiori pass.
Bukayo Saka scored Arsenal's second goal after strong buildup play involving Declan Rice and Christos Tzolis.
Martin Odegaard scored the third goal with a scuffed shot, capping off a stellar performance.
Arsenal kept a clean sheet as goalkeeper David Raya was barely tested during the match.

title: Arsenal v Coventry City: Premier League – live
author: Scott Murray
content:
52 min: Rushworth redeems himself by tipping a fiercely whipped Lewis-Skelly curler over the bar. That was heading into the top left. Coventry are really hanging on now.
50 min: Odegaard celebrated that one sheepishly. He knows it’s really on the keeper. But it was another smooth Arsenal move. They’re putting it together tonight.
Saka feeds White on the overlap out on the right. White reaches the byline and cuts back from Odegaard, who has to score from eight yards … and does, but only after scuffing a shot towards the bottom right that should be stopped. However Rushworth, diving the wrong way, flaps a weak hand at the ball, which apologetically rolls over the line.
This could very messy for Coventry. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty Images
48 min: Thomas-Asante runs purposefully down the inside-left channel and looks to have been skittled unnecessarily by White, just outside the area. But he’s not getting the free kick. Coventry livid, as is krishnamoorthy v, who splutters: “Saka talking during half time!? What next? Hydration breaks and cheerleaders with pom poms?”
47 min:Arsenal start the second half as they finished the first, by hogging the ball. They’re in total control of this, and have been ever since the 48-second mark. In other news, here’s Justin Kavanagh: “I notice Arteta is starting the new season in the driver’s seat, so to speak, in much more relaxed-fit, extra-length pants than last season’s school uniform variety. He’s earned a breather.
Arsenal get the second half started. No changes. Meanwhile Andrew Goudie, age undefined, writes: “Just to reinforce your demographic profile. A friend of mine told me that he once went to Highfield Road and realised at the turnstile that he hadn’t brought any cash. In a panic, he asked if they would take a cheque, which they did.”
Bukayo Saka has a half-time chat with Sky Sports, because yes, football has come to this. “It’s a great start from us … we’ve had a great 45 minutes … we’ve played really well … flowed well … the Arsenal we want to see this season … we want more … we want to score more goals … that’s the attitude we’re gonna come back out with.”
Half-time postbag. “A Frank Lampard team in the Premier League looking bright going forward but far too open and easy to score against going the other way? I, for one, am shocked” – Louwrens Botha
“I am sure the pundits will slag Coventry as not being worthy of the Premier League but Arsenal is going do this to many opponents this year. Look at what they did to Man City. They are a wagon” – Mary Waltz
“Uncontroversial Comment of the Evening: Arsenal looking pretty good” – Charles Antaki
45 min +1: … Odegaard wins another with a speculative shot that’s deflected right. And from the second corner of the sequence, Rice is afforded far too much time out on the right, and curls powerfully towards the top left. Rushworth isn’t necessarily getting to the shot, even at full stretch, but the ball drifts wide.
45 min: OK, well scrub that. Tzolis bustles in from the left and prepares to shoot, only to be clumsily clanked by Yirenkyi, who having already been booked wants to watch himself here. The referee waves play on, and Odegaard wins a corner on the right. From which …
42 min: Tchaouna, who has been Coventry’s brightest attacker, to undeservedly damn with faint praise, nearly halves the deficit in spectacular style. Taking up possession with his back to goal on the edge of the Arsenal D, he hooks a gentle overhead up, down and towards the top-right corner. It very nearly beats Raya, who backtracks in a panic, but the ball just clears the crossbar and lands on the top of the net. What a goal that would have been!
41 min: I can’t be the only viewer of a certain vintage who occasionally squints at the camera and convinces himself that the red sponsorship on Coventry’s shirt reads GRANADA BINGO … just because I want that to be the case?
39 min: No penalty. The shot fairly clearly hit Van Ewijk on the back. Maybe a smidgen of elbow, but it was tucked into his body, and the defender wasn’t even facing the ball.
38 min: … and the ball’s cut back for Calafiori, who shoots into a crowded box. It’s blocked and cleared … but VAR wants to check for a possible penalty.
35 min: Grimes curls the free kick to the far post, where Mosquera clears easily enough, Yirenkyi behind him, waiting to power a header goalwards. Arsenal break upfield, and Tzolis is fairly crudely shoulder-barged to the floor by Van Ewijk, who is fortunate not to go into the book.
34 min: … and now he brings down Simms, who spins him on the left. A free kick, just outside the box, and a booking for Gabriel, who is now grimacing for a totally different reason.
Gabriel goes into the book for a foul on Ellis Simms on the edge of the box. Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images
33 min: Gabriel may be having a bit of bother with the foot Simms stood on. He’s wolfed down a painkiller, and is flinching a little bit whenever he kicks the ball.
29 min: Coventry settle down a little bit, and string together a few passes in the Arsenal half. Tchaouna at the heart of most of it. They don’t really advance much, but that’s not really the point with the game in its current state. Small acorns.
27 min: Lewis-Skelly barges Yirenkyi off the ball. Coventry’s new midfielder tries to win it back, but only manages to clatter his in-flight opponent from behind, and into the book he goes.
Myles Lewis-Skelly is fouled by Caleb Yirenkyi. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images
25 min:Arsenal stroke the ball around the back awhile. Very patient. Then a long pass down the right that nearly releases White, who is nudged by Dasilva. White goes over, demanding the free kick, but he’s not getting one. Arsenal looking so dangerous, though.
It’s going to be a long night for everyone in blue and white. Rice bombs forward and slips the ball to the irrepressible Tsolis on the left. Tsolis crosses low and hard. Rushworth gets down to palm the ball away from Havertz, but only manages to wrong-foot his defenders and tee up Saka, who can’t miss, tapping home from a couple of yards.
Bukayo Saka taps home as the champions show their class. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images
21 min: Saka dribbles hard at Dasilva again, reaching the box before finding White infield. White shuttles the ball on for Lewis-Skelly, who can’t get a shot away quick enough. Another slick move, though, and it looks like being a long night for poor old Dasilva.
19 min: It’s all Arsenal. Coventry go on a rare sortie upfield, Simms chasing a pass down the left. He accidentally stands on Gabriel’s foot, and play stops for the defender to grimace and hop around a bit. He’ll be OK to continue.
17 min: Frank Lampard had been on the touchline, seconds before the goal, pleased with the way his team had started out at the home of the champions. He came to the edge of the pitch and applauded. But seconds later his mood went south. Incidentally, it was nice of Arsenal to have waited just long enough for us to get that bottling callback (12 min) in.
Van Ewijk fluffs a clearance near the left-hand corner flag. He’s closed down. Calafiori takes up possession and crosses low for Havertz, who sweeps majestically into the bottom right. What a finish! The champions up and running in short order!
Kai Havertz sweeps home and the champions lead. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters
12 min: From the resulting corner, Saka delivers straight into Rushworth’s arms. No score yet, so as per Harry Christie’s pre-match email, we have to ask: are Arsenal bottling this league challenge?
11 min: Saka drives at Dasilva down the right and crosses from a tight angle. Dasilva sticks out a boot and deflects behind, the ball nearly sneaking into the top right from a really tight angle.
9 min: Tzolis is everywhere. Here he is down the left again, this time cutting back for Rice, who balloons an effort over the bar from long range. The champions look up for this.
8 min: … the ball’s worked in triangles back down the right, then across the face of the Coventry box for White, whose forensic sidefoot towards the bottom left is cleared by the already-busy Thomas. Lovely move, and not your usual Arsenal corner routine.
7 min: Tzolis races down the right this time, and cuts back for Saka, whose chest-down-and-hit is deflected wide right by Thomas. And from that corner …
6 min: Tzolis drives down the left, cuts infield, goes back a little, then on the edge of the box swivels and sends a fierce rising drive over the bar. That was travelling, and not all that far away from the top-right corner. Rushworth might have had it covered.
Christos Tzolis has an early sighter for Arsenal. Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty Images
4 min:Arsenal fans give their Champions of England song the first run out of the season. You know how it goes: we know what they are. Meanwhile Fulham fan Richard Hirst sends in an email headed “Realism corner”. Yes, it’s come to this already. “On the basis that we face Chelsea, Liverpool and Man Utd in our first five games, Fulham need to make sure that there are at least three teams below us at that point. So come on Arsenal go large, goal difference could matter. (It’s never too early to panic!)”
Mikel Arteta and Frank Lampard hug it out … there’s a blast of that anthem … then Coventry get the ball rolling. Rushworth launches long … and within 17 seconds, Tchaouna wins the first corner of the season with a determined run down the right! They couldn’t, could they?
The hosts welcome their NEW!!! signing Ezri Konsa … and then tonight’s teams emerge from the tunnel. A wild and wonderful pyro-party atmosphere at the home of the NEW!!! champions. Arsenal are in their NEW!!! red and white shirts while Coventry sport their NEW!!! blue and white striped tops. Gotta love the start of the season. Excited, yes? “Arsenal fan here,” answers Harry Christie. “After finally getting over the line last year, some savvy recruitment in the summer and in a year where approximately half the league is in a state of flux, if Arsenal start the season slowly at what point do we reckon the ‘bottling it’ talk will commence? My money’s on somewhere around the 12th minute tonight.” We’ll be off once the pre-match pleasantries have been concluded.
The Emirates crowd welcome new signing Ezri Konsa. Photograph: John Walton/PA
Pre-season postbag: moaning about the state of modern television and pop music (which kind of gives away our demographic but what are you gonna do?) edition. “Almost as good as the music from those Granada Football titles is the variety in the clips. There’s fouls, bad control, close misses, mud, as well as a couple of goals. The people who put that together clearly had a much better understanding of the game than those who think all we’re interested in is seeing the ball hitting the net” – David Wall
“I saw a very early Kasabian at Brixton Academy, sandwiched between the Cooper Temple Clause and Black Rebel Motorcycle Club. Both of whom were much more entertaining. They were toilet then, and they’re toilet now. But in fairness, they have since been tremendously successful, if a little one-dimensional. Entirely unrelated, Arsenal surely can’t do it again. I’m predicting a battling third-place finish for them” – Matt Dony
Pre-season postbag: football edition. “Arsenal and Coventry means only one thing to me. Boxing Day 1999, Coventry 3 Arsenal 2. Robbie Keane scored the most impudent of goals. It probably doesn’t stick out for other people but my parents had finally got Sky (Christmas present) and this was one of the first matches that I watched at home and it has stayed with all these years. Strange how something so inconsequential can stay in the memory for some reason like that” – John Brennan
“How to take on this Arsenal? Well it is kind of straight forward. Look at what Arsenal does when their press is broken: they drop into a 4-4-2 (11 behind the ball) such that any ball carrier will always be running at two defenders. If Arsenal wide men (Tzolis, Madueke) get a run at single defenders, Coventry is going to get diced. If Coventry keep two on ones everywhere, the only Arsenal player that can reliably beat a double team is 16 years old. 0-0. Well done Sky Blues!” – Drew Lundgren
“It is so great to have Premier League football back so, at least for a moment, we have something to take our minds off of the hellscape we live in today. Will Coventry get blitzed? Of course, but it will be fun anyway” – Mary Waltz
Coventry City goal machine Micky Quinn celebrates after scoring a hat-trick against Arsenal on the opening day of the 1993/94 season at Highbury. Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images
Mikel Arteta’s turn to talk pitchside to Sky. “The players need that desire to go again … I certainly have it … we have to create an opportunity … we don’t know what other clubs are going to do … we have to be the best version of ourselves … we have to deliver our game for 96 minutes every three days … if you are not capable of doing that, you are in trouble … we have to get better … we are trying to improve the team [in the transfer window] … but so far I am very happy.”
He also reports that Bruno Guimarães “had a slight tension in his groin … he did not have a pre-season … we need to take him bit by bit.”
Coventry manager Frank Lampard speaks to Sky Sports. “It means a great deal … the story of 25 years … what the fans were desperate for … we’ve managed to bring that back to the club … amazing, but now reality’s here and we’re driving up to the Emirates … I love it … the top level … the team that got us here deserve it … you’re gonna play Arsenal away at some point in the season … our season will not be defined by this game … we need to keep the balance … of course we had to add to it … we’re happy with what we’ve done … hopefully that’ll show on the pitch.”
Arsenal make two changes to the side that started the 3-0 Community Shield rout of Manchester City. Bukayo Saka and Declan Rice replace Noni Madueke, who is benched, and the injured Bruno Guimarães, who is expected to be missing for a few weeks after picking up a thigh problem at Wembley. Christos Tzolis makes his Premier League debut.
Coventry City have a few debutants on their teamsheet. Swiss defender Aurèle Amenda, Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi and French winger Loum Tchaouna start, while Taiwo Awoniyi, this week’s signing from Nottingham Forest, and Gustavo Hamer, newly returned from Sheffield United, are on the bench.
BREAKING NEWS: Sky Sports are still using that indefensible Kasabian racket for their Premier League theme tune. Bah. Had been very much hoping they’d replace it for the new campaign. Me, I’d pop the master tapes in the nearest brazier, and instead whack on Magic Trumpet by Herb Alpert and the Tijuana Brass, last used in this specific context by Granada Television for their gloriously Soviet-branded late-60s programme FOOTBALL. Tell me this wouldn’t improve your mood at least tenfold every time you heard it.
More classic sporting themes in this old Joy of Six, if you can be bothered.
… so let’s start at the very beginning. One step before the beginning, in fact. The Guardian presents, for your edification, the Premier League 2026-27 previews for Arsenal and Coventry City. Just in case you missed them.
The Premier League is back, and you won’t get too many people making a case for newly promoted Coventry City to get something in tonight’s opening game against champions Arsenal. But then on the first day of the 1993-94 season, Micky Quinn did this …
… and there weren’t too many at Highbury expecting that either. Throw in that Lee Dixon own goal, the centrepiece of another early-season away win for Cov, this time in 1991-92 with Arsenal reigning champions, and the Sky Blues have some disruptive form here. On the other hand, that was over 30 years ago, and Arsenal have won all five of the meetings between these clubs in the 21st century, albeit the last of those being in 2014. So take your pick as the champions of England meet the winners of the Championship. Kick-off is at 8pm BST. It’s back, and it’s on!
summary: Arsenal dominates possession and controls the match against Coventry City in a Premier League fixture. Goals from Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard give the champions a commanding lead after capitalizing on defensive errors. Coventry struggles to contain Arsenal's fluent attacks while creating very few scoring opportunities of their own.
key_points: Kai Havertz opened the scoring with a low sweep into the bottom right corner following a Coventry clearance error.
Martin Odegaard scored Arsenal's second goal after a mistake by Coventry goalkeeper Rushworth.
Coventry's best attacking moment came when Tchaouna narrowly missed with an overhead shot that landed on top of the net.
Arsenal maintained total control of the match and dominated possession from the early stages of the game.

Arsenal vs Coventry preview
Premier League champions Arsenal took just 23 seconds to seize command in Sunday’s statement win over Manchester City in the Community Shield and the Gunners’ title defence should start with a routine victory over Coventry at the Emirates.
Mikel Arteta’s men were crowned Premier League champions for the first time in 22 years last season, finishing seven points clear at the summit, and the manner of their Community Shield success over City has only strengthened their position as favourites to repeat their title heroics.
Arsenal’s recent success has been defined by an impenetrable backline and that was the case again during the 3-0 win at the Principality Stadium, where a desperate City were forced to unleash five of their 12 shots from outside the box.
Starting defenders Jurrien Timber and William Saliba were missing through injury but Ben White and Cristhian Mosquera stepped in to highlight the Gunners’ strength in depth defensively and they were already in command once Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka were introduced from the bench.
The Gunners have had the best defensive record in the last three Premier League seasons. They conceded only 29 goals in chasing City home in the 2023-24 campaign while they were breached just 27 times in getting over the line last term.
Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya kept 19 clean sheets last season and they opened the 2025-26 campaign with a hard-fought 1-0 win at Manchester United, where they were second-best but stood firm.
Arteta’s side won four of their first five home games to nil last season, conceding only in a 1-1 draw against City, and they won five of their six meetings with promoted clubs Leeds, Burnley and Sunderland without conceding.
That shows the challenge that Coventry may face in creating chances and there is no tougher starting point for last season’s Championship winners, who are back in the Premier League for the first time since 2001.
After a mid-season wobble, Frank Lampard’s men turned it back on to finish 11 points clear of Ipswich but they won only five of their final 14 away league games.
Business has been done in an attempt to secure survival but last season’s top scorer Haji Wright and star winger Ephron Mason-Clark have endured pre-season setbacks and are doubts at the Emirates.
Loum Tchaouna has arrived from Burnley but he scored just twice in the Premier League last term while Taiwo Awoniyi, who joins from Nottingham Forest, featured only 17 times in last season’s top flight.
This is a rise in class for players such as Ellis Simms, Brandon Thomas-Asante and Tatsuhiro Sakamoto and that suggests the visitors may struggle to breach one of the most structured and controlled teams in world football.
Hitman Havertz to put Coventry to the sword
Viktor Gyokeres established himself in two full Championship campaigns at Coventry before sealing a move to Sporting and he was Arsenal’s top scorer in the Premier League last season with 14 goals.
However, the Swedish international may have to wait to inflict pain on his former side as Kai Havertz should win the battle to lead the line.
Havertz started in the Community Shield win over City, scoring the second goal, and was replaced by Gyokeres with only 15 minutes remaining.
Injuries impacted the start of Havertz’s campaign last season but he scored in four of Arsenal’s final six Champions League matches, which included the defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in the final, and he bagged three goals in four World Cup appearances for Germany.
Havertz registered four goal contributions in his final five Premier League appearances last season and he could set the Gunners on their way.

title: World Cup 2026: Argentina's Paredes banned for 10 games over World Cup final clashes
author: Alex Brotherton; Simon Stone
content:
![Paredes](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/4619/live/4e75a6e0-9d6f-11f1-bdcc-8926c4a74c43.jpg)
Paredes plays his club football for Argentinian side Boca Juniors
- Published
Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes has been given a 10-match ban for the role he played in on-field clashes after his side were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
Fifa's disciplinary committee has also handed his team-mate Nahuel Molina a seven-match suspension.
Argentina have also been ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, though one match of that sanction is suspended.
The Argentinian Football Association (AFA) has been fined $321,000 (Â£235,000) for breaches of the Fifa disciplinary code relating to using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.
Fifa have ordered that $100,000 (Â£73,000) of the fine must be invested in a plan to combat discrimination - and $100,000 (Â£73,000) of the fine is suspended, with a probationary period to apply.
After defeating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner claiming Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory.
Last month, Fifa appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at the New York New Jersey Stadium, when multiple Argentina players and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players.
As well as their suspensions, Paredes and Molina will both pay fines of $90,000 (Â£66,000).
Paredes grabbed Eric Garcia by the throat and wrestled Spain's Gavi to the ground, before appearing to strike the latter in the face.
Gavi - who said he did not think Paredes should be punished - will serve a one-match suspension and pay a fine of $30,000 (Â£22,000) for his part in the post-match confrontations, as will Argentina's Thiago Almada.
Roberto Ayala, a member of Argentina's coaching staff, has been given a three-match suspension and a fine of $30,000 for striking Spain's Dani Olmo in the face.
The match suspensions will only be enforced in international fixtures.
The AFA said it will appeal the sanctions, and if unsuccessful will take its case to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
Analysis: Fifa come down hard on Argentina
There were many elements of Argentina's behaviour around the World Cup final that left a sour taste â now world governing body Fifa has come down hard on those it feels were responsible.
A 10-match ban for experienced central midfielder Paredes and seven matches for Molina, who seemed to punch man of the match Rodri as he ran to celebrate Spain's success.
In addition, the fine of $321,000 includes a punishment for the Argentina team unveiling a "Las Malvinas son ÂArgentinas" â the ÂMalvinas are Argentinian â banner following their semi-final triumph against England.
It is a significant punishment, underlining how annoyed Fifa are at having their showpiece occasion, broadcast to an estimated 1.5bn people globally, tarnished by such awful scenes.
Argentina have been one of the world's best teams for some time. Today shows them to be one of the worst behaved.
summary: Fifa has handed Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes a 10-match ban and teammate Nahuel Molina a seven-match suspension following on-field clashes after the 2026 World Cup final against Spain. The Argentinian Football Association was also fined $321,000 for team misconduct, discriminatory chants, and displaying a political banner regarding the Falkland Islands after their semi-final match. Additionally, various fines and suspensions were issued to other players and coaching staff involved in the altercations.
key_points: Leandro Paredes received a 10-match ban and a $90,000 fine for his involvement in post-match clashes with Spain.
Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven matches and fined $90,000.
The Argentinian Football Association was fined $321,000 for team misconduct, discriminatory chants, and non-sporting demonstrations.
Argentina was ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, with one match of the sanction suspended.
The AFA announced plans to appeal the sanctions to Fifa and potentially the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

title: England beat Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs: first men’s cricket Test, day three – live reaction
author: Rob Smyth; Tim de Lisle; Taha Hashim
content:
Ali Martin has filed his match report, no messing about, so that’s my cue to go and get some fresh air. Thanks for your company, correspondence and views on the reviews. It’s been the thumping victory England fans wanted, and the one Pakistan fans feared. The Root-Trescothick regime, makeshift as it is, has got off to an excellent start.
The Sky pundits are discussing the result. Have we learnt anything about England, asks Ian Ward. “Not really,” says Stuart Broad. “Joe Root won an important toss. I know Pakistan said they would have batted but I sometimes think that’s a bit of a mind game… You bowl first, you win the game here for the past six or seven years… '[But] you can only beat what’s in front of you and England have done that quite comprehensively. If you win a Test by an innings and 100 runs, against anyone, it’s a strong performance. They caught really well… The only person who you look at and think ‘it hasn’t gone his way at all’ is Jamie Smith.”
“The biggest thing is Joe Root,” says Nasser Hussain. “He had a really good three days. The way he batted, the way he captained in the field. It was never ‘look at me’, it was never ‘I’m being Ben Stokes,’ it was just Joe being Joe with a smile on his face. He was much better here than he was at the Oval.”
And here’s Joe Root, the winning captain – we haven’t been able to say that for a while. As is his wont, he deflects the praise. Very skilful,” he says, of the bowling. “I thought the bowlers found the right areas very early on in the Test and once we got ahead, we showed great maturity actually… It’s very exciting to see a complete performance.”
When Mark Butcher asks about the batting, Root praises Jordan Cox’s calmness at No 3 and adds, “Brooky showed why he’s the best player in the world.”
And his own batting? “I love batting for England and that’s never really gonna waver.” But getting out when he did “wasn’t great example-setting from me”. As always, he radiates decency. And his captaincy here was much sharper than it was back in the day, or even at the Oval in June.
Here’s Salman Ali Agha, Pakistan’s stand-in captain, and he doesn’t gild the lily. “England have outplayed us,” he says. “We have made many mistakes… we need to come back stronger… Ali Usman was outstanding… We need to go to London and sit down [and talk about it], and hopefully Babar comes back.”
The player-of-the-match trophy could easily be shared by Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue, and cut in half. But there’s no need for the saw after all, as it goes to Robinson. “I didn’t feel in great rhythm [at first],” he says, ”but it was nipping both ways and I knew as long as I could control my length and my line, I was in the game…”
Joe Root will dominate the headlines, and he deserves to after taking the reins again. But Mark Wood is making a good point: that credit should also go to the backroom staff, led by Marcus Trescothick, who held a meeting with the seamers this morning. Wood feels the message will have been to concentrate on wobble-seam, which worked a treat.
The first email to arrive since the end of the game is an interesting one. “Excellent umpiring throughout,” says Andrew Goudie. “England poor with reviews.”
True, but perhaps we can agree that they got away with it?
Fun fact: Josh Tongue took his eight wickets here off only 15 overs. That’s a wicket every 11 balls. In his previous Test, the grievous loss to New Zealand at Trent Bridge, he bowled 35 overs and took none for 150. If he’d bowled as well in that series as he did here, Ben Stokes might still be the England captain.
To win a Test, you (nearly always) have to take 20 wickets. Joe Root’s new-look England managed it in 85 overs, 84 of them bowled by their four seamers, who took all 20. Eight each to Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue, three to Jofra Archer and one to Gus Atkinson.
37th over: Pakistan 131-9 (Abbas 2, Mohammad Ali 0) So, just the rabbits left now, and nobody in the hutch.
“Where does this sit in the ‘one team poor, the other good’ scale, Tim?” asks Guy Hornsby. “It’s great to see this England attack making hay, and wickets and pressure shared between the whole group, but it’s hard to assess things when Pakistan look so feeble.” True, and the point about sharing also applies to the runs.
“As much as I want us to win this series, seeing Pakistan so rickety always gives me a tinge of sadness. They’re better than this. But Tongue, Robinson, Atkinson and Archer will not care one jot. England do seem to have a real depth, and that’s not been the case for some time.”
Well … one shocker doesn’t make a summer. Look at New Zealand, who lost the first Test by a distance and still won the series. But yes, Pakistan are in a bad way, and it’s not hard to picture them being whitewashed.
36th over: Pakistan 129-8 (Rizwan 39, Abbas 2) Rizwan takes a single off the first ball of Robinson’s over, just as he did, fatally, when batting with Khurram. This time the rabbit at the other end survives, because Abbas isn’t quite good enough to get a nick.
35th over: Pakistan 128-8 (Rizwan 38, Abbas 2) After seeing him go for 26 off two overs, Joe Root takes Josh Tongue off in disgust. He brings back Atkinson, who manages to keep Rizwan relatively quiet, but still has no wicket in the match.
34th over: Pakistan 125-8 (Rizwan 35, Abbas 2) Robinson, bowling to Abbas, restores order with a maiden. Abbas, as he heads for a mid-pitch chat with Rizwan, looks chuffed to have survived it.
“There are some good bowling figures all over the country this week,” says Rob Knap, “but I think Ben Allison’s for Worcs at Gloucs are the most pleasing (if you’re into this kind of thing): 17.5-9-19-5. A week or so after the six-hitting competition ended, it’s really lovely to see.”
A nice point. But to be fair, the six-hitting competition involved plenty of good bowling. And some of it came from three of England’s bowlers here – Josh Tongue, Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson, who has bowled better than his figures might suggest.
33rd over: Pakistan 125-8 (Rizwan 35, Abbas 2) Tongue puts a foot wrong in a small way, letting Abbas take a single off the first ball. Rizwan tucks in – a crisp cover drive for two, a rasping pull for four. That takes him to the top score in the innings, for what it’s worth: he celebrates this dubious milestone with a straight drive for four more. Tongue bites back with a fast length ball that hits Rizwan on the inner thigh. Ouch! But Rizwan has put a dent in Tongue’s figures, which have suddenly gone from 5-0-17-3 to 7-0-43-3.
32nd over: Pakistan 114-8 (Rizwan 25, Abbas 1) So Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue took five wickets apiece in the first innings, and now they’ve got three each in the second. Test cricket, so hard so often, can sometimes be strangely easy.
WICKET! Pakistan 111-8 (Khurram c Cox b Robinson 8)
Rizwan exposes Khurram again, this time after only one ball of Robinson’s over. I just don’t know what’s going off out there. Khurram edges the next delivery straight to third slip to give Robinson his eighth wicket of the match.
Ollie Robinson is congratulated on dismissing Pakistan's Kharrum Shahzad. Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/Shutterstock
31st over: Pakistan 110-7 (Rizwan 22, Khurram 8) A loose delivery from Tongue is pinged through square leg for four by Rizwan, who then takes a single to leave Khurram with three deliveries to survive. Not sure about that tactic. Khurram is dropped, technically, when Cox gets a fingertip on a desperately difficult chance at third slip. Another edge flies through the slips for four more.
“It seems to me that amongst all the hyper-criticism of the BazBall era, one fairly big factor in its decline was overlooked,” writes Phil Harrison. “England lost Broad, Anderson and Woakes in the space of two years. That’s a huge thing and it’s no wonder it’s caused them to struggle – remember how Australia went back into the pack when Warne and McGrath retired in quick succession. Could it be that we’re only just now starting to plug those gaps?”
30th over: Pakistan 95-7 (Rizwan 15, Khurram 0) That was a nice catch from Cox, who reacted quicker than anyone when the ball looped up off Smith’s thigh. In a related development, Tongue and Robinson have taken 15 of the 17 wickets to fall.
Ollie Robinson strikes with the first ball of a new spell. Ali Usman snicked him onto the thigh of Smith, standing up to the stumps, and Jordan Cox ran in from third slip to snaffle the rebound.
Ollie Robinson celebrates with teammates after taking the wicket of Ali Usman. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters
29th over: Pakistan 95-6 (Rizwan 15, Usman 7) Tongue has a big LBW appeal against Usman turned down. England lose a review on an appeal that didn’t look quite right; Usman was outside the line of off stump.
28th over: Pakistan 93-6 (Rizwan 14, Usman 6) A terrific bumper from Archer hits Usman on the shoulder. Usman responds nicely with a square drive for four later in the over.
27th over: Pakistan 88-6 (Rizwan 13, Usman 2) Rizwan is good enough to push Tongue down the ground for four. He’s beaten for pace next ball and deflects it past the stumps for a single. Tongue is bowling ferociously. It’s not as primal as some fast-bowling spells because he’s attacking the stumps rather than the head, but it’s still quite thrilling to watch.
26th over: Pakistan 83-6 (Rizwan 8, Usman 2) Exemplary channel bowling from Archer, who beats Ali Usman four times in a row. He appealed for caught behind after the third; it brushed the hip rather than the outside edge.
25th over: Pakistan 83-6 (Rizwan 8, Usman 2) Never mind Test matches, Tongue hasn’t taken a ten-for in first-class cricket. His best figures are 9 for 98, it says here.
Pakistan have a long tail so there’s a luscious whiff of rabbit pie wafting round Headingley. It’s not fair to include Ali Usman in that – he has a first-class hundred – and he faces four deliveries of that Tongue over without alarm.
It’s the senior batter, Rizwan, who almost falls when an inside-edge deflects past the stumps.
24th over: Pakistan 80-6 (Rizwan 7, Usman 0) You know somebody is bowling well when Jofra Archer’s overs at the other end feel like filler. Muhammad Rizwan hits a boundary, that’s about it.
Josh Tongue has taken a wicket every 8.2 balls in this game. No bowler in Test history has taken eight or more wickets in a match with a better strike-rate. Not even George Lohmann.
It’s out! Salman Ali Agha was late on another rapid delivery that cut back to hit him on the knee roll. He was given out LBW on the field, reviewed in the hope it was going over the top. Almost, but not quite: it would have trimmed the bails and Tongue has his third wicket of the innings. Already.
This guy is a wicket-taking animal. Masood pushes at a snarling delivery from round the wicket that straightens to take the edge and is safely grabbed by Ben Duckett at first slip.
Rob Key has worn many a custard pie of late, so let’s give him some flowers for picking Josh Tongue when Tongue was a Division Two bowler with a dismal average. What a bowler!
21st over: Pakistan 68-4 (Masood 28, Salman 0) There is precedent for deliberately bowling outside leg stump, particularly to left-handers - the Aussies had a fair bit of success against David Gower with that tactic – and England celebrated like a team who had pulled a rabbit out of the hat. Either that or they couldn’t believe their luck.
WICKET! Pakistan 68-4 (Saud c Lawrence b Tongue 14)
Josh Tongue strikes in his first over. He couldn’t bowl a wicketless spell if he tried. Saud Shakeel, who played a gorgeous straight drive for four earlier in the over, flicked a leg-stump delivery straight to Dan Lawrence at a kind of wide short fine leg.
Was Tongue bowling for that? The delivery was well outside leg stump, and Lawrence was in an unusual position for exactly that shot. Who knows.
20th over: Pakistan 64-3 (Masood 28, Saud 10) Saud Shakeel starts the afternoon with a leisurely on-drive for four from Archer’s second ball. If you’ve got it, flaunt it.
19th over: Pakistan 59-3 (Masood 28, Saud 5) Atkinson and Masood give each other nothing in the final over of the morning session. The result is another maiden, Atkinson’s fourth in six overs.
That was a pretty good morning for England, who extended their lead to 238 before taking three early wickets. Pakistan have a helluva lot to do if they are to make a game of this.
18th over: Pakistan 59-3 (Masood 28, Saud 5) Dan Lawrence gets a single over before lunch, the first by an England spinner in this match. He’s an occasional spinner, with a first-class average of 47, but he does turn the ball and he starts here with a decent maiden to Shakeel.
“For some lunchbreak reading,” begins Krishnamoorthy V, “may I offer this?”
Indeed you may, and thanks for sending it in. Batting techniques are a hot topic, and it feels like a very good time to be interrogative seam bowler.
17th over: Pakistan 59-3 (Masood 28, Saud 5) Masood is beaten by successive deliveries from Atkinson. The first was a jaffa, the second a loose shot that was probably caused by the first. Atkinson does Masood on the inside with the final ball of the over.
Another maiden from Atkinson, who has quietly bowled a fine spell of 5-3-6-0.
14th over: Pakistan 53-3 (Masood 28, Saud 1) Saud Shakeel tries to pull his first ball and almost drags it onto the stumps.
Robinson took Test-best match figures of 7 for 77 on his comeback earlier in the summer. He could improve upon them here: his current match figures are 6 for 71.
WICKET! Pakistan 51-3 (Shafique c Brook b Robinson 15)
Ollie Robinson strikes! Shafique pushes defensively at a terrific delivery, bowled from wider of the crease, that straightens sharply to take the edge. Harry Brook does the rest at second slip. The line and length were so good.
Ollie Robinson and his team-mates celebrate the wicket of Abdullah Shafique. Photograph: Matt West/Shutterstock
13th over: Pakistan 51-2 (Masood 27, Shafique 15) Shafique drives Atkinson pleasantly through the covers for a couple, with three singles following later in the over.
In other news, Ben Stokes made a rapid 53 for Durham in the County Championship and Olly Stone has nailed Ollie Pope for nought. Tanya Aldred has all the details.
12th over: Pakistan 46-2 (Masood 26, Shafique 11) Jofra Archer is replaced by Ollie Robinson rather than Josh Tongue. It’s an unusually poor over from Robinson, with T-W-O loose deliveries that are both cut for four by Masood.
Though Pakistan are still in all sorts, this pair have found a nice balance between attack and defence.
11th over: Pakistan 38-2 (Masood 18, Shafique 11) England go up for LBW whenA big nipbacker hits Shafique between the legs. It was too high, going down as well, and the discussion about a potential review is a brief one.
Atkinson is getting a bit of movement in the air and off the seam. An excellent, challenging maiden gives Shafique no scope to counter-attack.
I’m not saying he’s the second coming of Pat Cummins, but the best version of Atkinson – the one that bowled that over – is seriously good.
10th over: Pakistan 38-2 (Masood 18, Shafique 11) Archer tempts Masood with a wide, very full outswinger. Masood can’t resist a flashing drive and is beaten.
That’ll probably be it for this Archer spell: 5-0-27-2. No need to work him too hard when you have the bovver boy, Josh Tongue, waiting to come on.
9th over: Pakistan 36-2 (Masood 17, Shafique 10) Gus Atkinson comes on for Ollie Robinson, who bowled a pretty good opening spell of 4-1-10-0. His loosener (sic) is an absolute beauty that beats a wide-eyed Masood; the rest of the over passes without incident.
8th over: Pakistan 35-2 (Masood 16, Shafique 10) Shafique slaps Archer up and over the slip cordon for four. He counter-attacked splendidly from No4 in the first innings and is trying to do the same here. Archer almost kiboshes that with an outrageous wobble-seam delivery that snaps past the outside edge.
The next ball beats the bat as well. Archer has bowled some jaffas (and one or two freebies) in a spell of 4-0-25-2.
summary: England secured a dominant victory over Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs on day three of the first men’s cricket Test under the new Root-Trescothick regime. England's four-man seam attack—led by standout performances from Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue, who each took eight wickets in the match—bowled Pakistan out twice within 85 overs. Stand-in Pakistan captain Salman Ali Agha admitted his side was thoroughly outplayed, while Joe Root praised his bowlers for a complete and mature performance.
key_points: England defeated Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs to take a 1-0 lead in the Test series.
Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue both claimed eight wickets each across the match, anchoring England's bowling attack.
All 20 Pakistan wickets were taken by England's four seamers in a combined total of 85 overs.
Pakistan stand-in captain Salman Ali Agha acknowledged that his team made many mistakes and was heavily outplayed.

title: Savinho transfer: Spurs agree £85m deal to sign Brazil forward from Manchester City
author: Lyall Thomas; Michael Bridge
content:
Savinho transfer: Spurs agree £85m deal to sign Brazil forward from Manchester City
Savinho is set to undergo a medical ahead of a an £85m move to Tottenham Hotspur from Manchester City; Spurs have already spent more than £200m this summer on six first-team players; Savinho started in seven of his 24 Premier League appearances last season
Friday 21 August 2026 14:35, UK
Tottenham Hotspur have agreed an £85m deal with Manchester City to sign Savinho.
Spurs will pay an initial £75m for the Brazil international, with a further £10m available in add-ons.
It is understood that £5m of the potential bonuses are effectively guaranteed, meaning City could receive at least £80m from the deal.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Tottenham news & transfers⚪
- Spurs fixtures & scores | FREE Spurs highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The 22-year-old is scheduled to have a medical with Tottenham on Friday afternoon.
Spurs also remain in talks with Man City over a separate deal for striker Omar Marmoush as they look to further strengthen their attacking options.
Savinho, who has played a bit-part role since joining Manchester City in 2024, started only seven of his 24 Premier League appearances last season, in which he scored once and set up two goals.
Tottenham have already spent more than £200m on six first-team players this summer. They spent £185m on two midfielders, Sandro Tonali and Matheus Fernandes, from Newcastle and West Ham respectively.
Jan Paul van Hecke joined from Brighton for £52m to replace Cristian Romero.
Marcos Senesi, Andy Robertson and Martin Dubravka all arrived on free transfers.
Meanwhile, Savinho's potential sale would be a club record for Man City, surpassing Julian Alvarez's £82m move to Atletico Madrid in the summer of 2024.
How are Spurs spending so much money?
At the start of the transfer window, Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge explained how Spurs are able to spend big this summer...
"We're told there are absolutely no concerns about falling foul of the Premier League's financial rules.
"The club is in great financial health after qualifying for Europe in 18 of the last 20 seasons. The revenue driven by the stadium is huge: boxing, concerts, NFL games - you name it.
"In fact, in the Deloitte Money League, the rankings show that Tottenham Hotspur have leapfrogged Chelsea to become the ninth richest club in the world with annual revenues of £549.2m.
"On top of that, Spurs are one of the clubs to benefit most from the Premier League's shift to squad cost ratio from PSR, which has just come into effect. But the reason we're seeing Spurs spend so much is a shift in strategy under new leadership.
"Daniel Levy left at the start of last season, and there's a real desire to spend the money to dine at the very top table.
"Now the new leadership and the owners promised fans, after avoiding relegation on the final day, that they would spend the club's revenue on the first team, and they are delivering on that."
Maresca: Savinho wanted to leave from day one
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has admitted that Savinho had made it clear all summer that he wanted to leave the Etihad.
Maresca prepares for a first season in charge of City following the departure of Pep Guardiola, who oversaw the club's most successful period over nine years.
In preparation, Maresca has seen the likes of Ballon d'Or and World Cup-winning midfielder Rodri join Barcelona, while an agreement is in place to see Savinho move to Tottenham, with Omar Marmoush also linked to the north London club.
Asked whether he tried to convince Rodri to stay, Maresca said:
"It is quite clear when the player wants to leave, then it is complicated to convince them to stay.
"It happened with Rodri and the same thing is happening with Savinho.
"Since day one, he has asked me that he wants to leave. So now we are waiting. But it's complicated.
"When the player is thinking that they need a new challenge, or they want to change because they probably want to go back to Spain, or they want to play more minutes or for a different reason. It becomes complicated then to convince them to stay."
'City will want to replace Savinho and Marmoush'
Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom:
"Both players [Savinho and Marmoush] are essentially surplus to requirements at Manchester City. It's been pretty apparent through the summer. Enzo Maresca has said that in the case of both players, they are very much entitled to stay and fight for their first-team place.
"But equally he understands, a bit like James Trafford, when a player wants to play first-team football and they're not guaranteed the starting shirt, then the club, if they receive an offer that's acceptable, will not stand in their way. That applies to both players.
"City would need to replace these players. They would definitely, I'd say, have to replace one. They would like to and would aim to replace two.
"But the transfer window is closing in less than a fortnight. These are big positions to fill so late in the window."
summary: Tottenham Hotspur has agreed an £85m deal with Manchester City to sign Brazil forward Savinho, who is scheduled to undergo a medical on Friday. The transfer fee consists of an initial £75m plus £10m in add-ons, with £5m of those bonuses effectively guaranteed. This potential sale would set a club record for Manchester City, surpassing their previous sale of Julian Alvarez.
key_points: Spurs agreed to an £85m deal for Savinho, consisting of £75m initially and £10m in add-ons.
Savinho started only seven of his 24 Premier League appearances for Manchester City last season.
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca stated that Savinho had wanted to leave the club since day one of the summer.
The potential sale of Savinho would break Manchester City's club-record outgoing transfer fee.

title: Dutch Grand Prix: Kim Antonelli leads McLaren's Lando Norris in first practice
author: Andrew Benson
content:
![Kimi Antonelli on track at Zandvoort](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/965/cpsprodpb/26dc/live/f9230980-9d55-11f1-aac2-870643eea2ac.jpg)
Kimi Antonelli leads Lewis Hamilton in the drivers' championship by 50 points
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli headed McLaren's Lando Norris in first practice at the Dutch Grand Prix.
Championship leader Antonelli was 0.121 seconds clear of Norris - who won the last race in Hungary before Formula 1's summer break - with the Italian's Mercedes team-mate George Russell just 0.004secs further adrift.
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who is 50 points behind 19-year-old Antonelli in the championship, was fourth fastest - 0.190secs off the pace.
Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc and the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri completed the top six.
There was an encouraging performance from the new Honda engine in the Aston Martin, with Fernando Alonso ending the session 12th fastest and 1.562secs down.
That appears at first sight to suggest the new engine is providing the 0.3-0.5secs gain in lap time for which Aston Martin had been hoping.
If so, it still leaves Honda some way behind the performance of the best engines - as the company itself admits - but it is a step forward from the first iteration of their power-unit Aston Martin have used until now.
Signs Honda are on the right track are what Alonso has been looking for as he ponders whether to stay in the sport beyond the end of the season.
Audi's Nico Hulkenberg was seventh, the quickest driver not to use the soft tyres, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly, the second Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completing the top 10.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen could manage only 11th fastest, while his team-mate Liam Lawson, promoted from Racing Bulls after regular driver Isack Hadjar broke his wrist while boxing, was 14th.
A number of teams have chassis upgrades, notably Ferrari, who have brought a new floor to this race weekend hoping they can deliver on the potential they showed in Hungary last time, but which frittered away through strategy and operational errors.
At Alpine, only Gasly has the team's first major upgrade for some time, while McLaren and Aston Martin also have small aerodynamic upgrades - McLaren's around the rear bodywork and wing, and Aston Martin's the front wing.
summary: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli set the pace in the first practice session at the Dutch Grand Prix, finishing ahead of McLaren's Lando Norris and Mercedes team-mate George Russell. Championship rival Lewis Hamilton finished fourth for Ferrari, while Fernando Alonso showed encouraging signs with Aston Martin's new Honda engine in 12th. Meanwhile, Red Bull's Max Verstappen could only manage the 11th fastest time.
key_points: Kimi Antonelli led the opening practice session at Zandvoort, 0.121 seconds ahead of Lando Norris.
George Russell finished third fastest, just behind Norris in the other Mercedes.
Fernando Alonso ended the session 12th, indicating potential performance gains from Aston Martin's new Honda engine.
Max Verstappen struggled to 11th place for Red Bull.
Several teams introduced upgrades for the weekend, including a new floor for Ferrari and aerodynamic updates for McLaren and Aston Martin.

title: England vs Pakistan live: Score and latest updates from first Test
author: Kieran Crichard; Nick Hoult; Scyld Berry; Will Macpherson; Tim Wigmore
content:
![Jofra Archer had Imam caught behind without scoring](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499027382_17873101049140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqdh23LgVXBEut1oOPkGpYSg-MRB09dNBuDCYZlGCxz_Y.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Jofra Archer had Imam caught behind without scoring](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499027382_17873101049140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqdh23LgVXBEut1oOPkGpYSg-MRB09dNBuDCYZlGCxz_Y.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
OVER 4: PAK 13/2 (Shafique 0 Masood 4)
Abdullah Shafique, who was by far Pakistan’s best batsman in the first innings, joins Masood in the middle with his side in real trouble. Archer bowls a beauty to him first up that just beats the outside edge.
Jofra Archer was taken off after two overs at the Football Stand End in the first innings. No danger of that this time. His last delivery was 91mph, but his line - far harder to leave than in the first innings - has been as important.
Wicket
Azan c Root b Archer 9 Azan has picked out the leg slip to absolute perfection. After his first boundary on English soil, Azan gets one on is pads and clips it straight to Root, who had positioned himself at slip. Great captaincy from Root, taking a leaf out of the Stokes captaincy book. FOW 13/2
![Joe Root takes a catch to dismiss Azan Awais](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499028385_17873107868310_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqf7y1lzytB1DEvIVIXvqqK_mJDQle8zhAnRj3nA8oxTY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
OVER 3: PAK 7/1 (Azan 3 Masood 4)
Off his ninth ball, Azan finally gets off the pair as he guides one behind point for three. Good fielding from Atkinson on the rope prevented the boundary. Azan will be a relieved man.
The slip cordon is packed with England well on top. This is tough for these Pakistan batsmen.
Wicket
Imam c Smith b Archer 0 Jofra Archer will open the bowling alongside Robinson and gets a wicket with his fifth ball. Imam tries to sway out of the way of a short delivery from Archer but does not drop his hands enough. It clips the glove and Smith takes an easy catch. Imam knows he has hit it and does not think about a review. The worst possible start for Pakistan. FOW 0/1
Jofra Archer wasn’t at his best in the first innings and seemed to struggle to readjust to the Test game after his Hundred exertions. But that wicket shows Archer at his most hostile best. Archer and Ollie Robinson have the makings of a terrific, complementary opening attack.
![Jofra Archer celebrates taking the wicket of Pakistan's Imam-ul-Haq](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499027614_17873101780860_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
OVER 1: PAK 0/0 (Azan 0 Imam 0)
As he did in the first innings, Ollie Robinson will start proceedings with the ball. Azan is not just on a pair but a king pair. He survives the first ball to get off a king pair but is still on a pair. He plays out a maiden from Robinson and is still not off the pair.
Don’t we all want Pakistan to make a substantial second innings - to see what speed Ollie Robinson musters in his third and fourth spell?
Poor Azan Awais. This is a painful pair to be sat on, with Ollie Robinson all over him like a cheap suit.
Pakistan’s second innings
Azan Awais and Imam-ul-Haq make their way out to the middle and the tourists have so much work ahead of them just to stay in this Test match. Azan will be hoping for a better start to this innings than the first having been dismissed off the first ball of the match. These are probably better batting conditions than they were two days ago when this pair came out to bat on day one.
England all out for 409
Tongue b Khurram 9 Tongue drills Khurram down the ground for four but is then beaten by the Pakistan seamer and England’s innings is brought to a close. After the first innings, England lead Pakistan by 238 runs and the tourists will have to bat so much better than they did first time around. Ali Usman walks off with the ball in his hand after his five-for. FOW 409 all out
![Josh Tongue bowled by Khurram Shahzad](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499027155_17873100684620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqcXLA0TNltAe_ihgyEu4tG-il7a1KV2STY3xRqqFt_No.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
OVER 89: ENG 403/9 (Archer 22 Tongue 4)
What a lovely way to get off the mark! Tongue drills Abbas back over his head for four and that boundary brings up England’s 400. Abbas follows that up with a beauty which beats Tongue’s outside edge and the off stump.
I reckon that Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue should ask the groundsman again, to cut up this second new ball, to commemorate their small but frolicsome tenth wicket stand - the finishing touches to England’s handsome first innings lead.
summary: England's first innings concluded at 409 all out, giving them a lead of 238 runs over Pakistan. In their second innings, Pakistan suffered a disastrous start, losing both openers early with the score at 13 for 2. Jofra Archer claimed both early wickets, dismissing Imam-ul-Haq for a duck and Azan Awais for 9.
key_points: England were bowled out for 409, establishing a first-innings lead of 238 runs.
Ali Usman claimed a five-wicket haul for Pakistan.
Pakistan slumped to 13-2 in their second innings early on.
Jofra Archer dismissed Imam-ul-Haq and Azan Awais with hostile bowling.

title: England vs Pakistan LIVE: First Test, day three, Headingley - cricket score, radio & video highlights
author: Live Reporting by Elizabeth Botcherby
content:
